lem-connected-plane-multigraph-euler-for:
## Statement

Let $G$ be a finite nonempty connected plane multigraph drawn in $\mathbb R^2$: vertices
are distinct points; each edge is a polygonal arc joining its endpoints; edge
interiors are pairwise disjoint and avoid every vertex; and loops and parallel
edges are allowed. A loop is an edge whose two endpoints are the same vertex,
with its interior otherwise embedded. A face is a connected component of the
complement of the drawing. If $V,E,F$ are the numbers of vertices, edges, and
faces, respectively, then

$$V-E+F=2.$$
def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-code:
## Definition

Let $P$ be the projection plane in an oriented $3$-sphere and let $n$ be the
unit viewing normal pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ so that $(u,v)$ is
a positive basis exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive ambient basis. A
**crossing code** has a
finite set $C$ of crossing labels and a finite set $D$ of **darts**, where a
dart is one directed half-edge incident to a crossing. A fixed-point-free
involution $\alpha:D\to D$ pairs the two ends of each edge: $\alpha^2=\mathrm{id}$
and $\alpha(d)\ne d$. A vertex map $v:D\to C$ records the crossing incident to
each dart. A **rotation system** is the permutation $\sigma$ whose cycles give
the clockwise order of darts at each crossing. Each crossing has four darts;
the two over-strand darts and the two under-strand darts are opposite in that
cyclic order. An arrow on each dart records whether its edge is directed into
or out of its incident crossing. The pairing $\alpha$ must join one incoming
end to one outgoing end. At a crossing, each opposite pair has one incoming
and one outgoing dart, so following an edge and then the opposite dart defines
the oriented link components. A code is **connected** when the graph with
vertices $C$ and edges the $\alpha$-pairs is connected.

The sign of an oriented crossing is $+1$ or $-1$ according as
$\det(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$ is positive or negative, where the two
tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. This item fixes
the local cyclic-order convention as follows. Starting with the outgoing
over-dart and reading counterclockwise, a positive crossing has order
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm out},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm in})$; a negative crossing has
order $(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$. The stored crossing
sign and cyclic order must agree. This is the page's explicit sign convention.
It agrees with the current KT-03 supplier: reversing its positive
counterclockwise order from outgoing over gives the clockwise record
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$.

For a nonempty connected crossing graph, let $V=|C|$, $E=|D|/2$, and let
$F$ be the number of cycles of the face permutation $\phi=\alpha\circ\sigma$.
A **spherical code** is a code satisfying $V-E+F=2$. A spherical code becomes a
**plane code** by distinguishing one face as the outer face and deleting a
point in that face from the sphere. The crossingless one-component code is a separate case: its Gauss data are one empty component word, its DT pairing and crossing-sign vector are empty at $c=0$, and its PD data are the single loop `Loop[1]`; every format also carries an orientation marker, `ccw` or `cw`, for the unit circle $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$ in the oriented plane, and the outer-face marker is `outside`. Thus the crossingless code records which direction orients its circle. It has no crossing graph or face-permutation test. Disconnected crossing graphs and disconnected crossingless links are outside this code class.

A **normalized planar-diagram code** with $c>0$ has crossing labels
$C=\{1,\ldots,c\}$ and four dart positions $0,1,2,3$ at each crossing, in
clockwise order beginning with the outgoing over-dart. The opposite pair
$(0,2)$ is over and $(1,3)$ is under. For sign $+1$, the clockwise record is
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm in},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm out})$; for sign $-1$ it is
$(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm out},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm in})$. Edge labels are assigned
by scanning crossings in increasing order and their four dart positions in
order, giving the next positive integer to the pair containing the first
not-yet-labelled dart. The outer face is recorded by its least dart in its
face cycle. These rules remove arbitrary edge-name and face-name choices;
different crossing labelings may still represent the same diagram. At $c=0$
a normalized code is the crossingless record with one of the two orientation
markers above.

A **Gauss code** for an oriented diagram records, in traversal order on each
oriented component, a signed crossing label: $+j$ means the component passes
over at crossing $j$, and $-j$ means it passes under. For a knot there is one
cyclic word; for a link there is one cyclic word per component. Each crossing
label must occur exactly twice in total, once positively and once negatively.
When $c>0$, every listed component word is nonempty; a separate crossingless
component is not part of this code class. The zero-crossing case is only the
one-component code specified above.
The code also carries a separate algebraic crossing-sign vector
$\varepsilon_j\in\{+1,-1\}$, one entry for each label. Choosing a basepoint
turns the knot's cyclic word into a based word; changing the basepoint
cyclically shifts the word, and relabeling crossings changes only their names.
The visit order, over/under signs, and crossing-sign vector determine the
crossing rotation system; it is realizable in the sphere only when the
resulting code is spherical. A plane Gauss code also carries an identifier of
one cycle of its face permutation to designate the outer face.

A **signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite code**, in this page's convention, encodes a
based oriented knot with $c$ crossings by numbering its $2c$ visits
$1,\ldots,2c$ in traversal order. For each odd visit $2j-1$, record the even
visit $2k$ paired with it as $d_j=+2k$ when the odd visit is over and
$d_j=-2k$ when it is under; also record the algebraic crossing sign
$\varepsilon_j\in\{+1,-1\}$ for crossing label $j$, the pair containing odd
visit $2j-1$. Its parity conditions are that
$|d_1|,\ldots,|d_c|$ are exactly the even numbers $2,4,\ldots,2c$, each once,
and each paired crossing has one over-visit and one under-visit. The separate
$\varepsilon_j$ records the crossing sign; signed DT conventions elsewhere
may encode signs differently. The associated cyclic traversal and crossing
signs determine a rotation system, which must pass the same spherical
realizability test. A plane DT code also carries an identifier of one cycle
of its face permutation to designate the outer face.

An **oriented planar-diagram code** labels each edge segment by an integer and
lists its two incident darts at crossing records. Each crossing record lists
its four directed edge ends in clockwise order, beginning with the outgoing
over-dart, and records which opposite pair is over, the orientation of each
strand, and the crossing sign. Every edge label occurs exactly twice, once as
an incoming end and once as an outgoing end. The code must satisfy the local
crossing-order rule above; its crossing graph must be connected when nonempty;
and its rotation system must satisfy $V-E+F=2$. The record also carries an
identifier of one cycle of its face permutation as the outer face. Thus an
arbitrary word in labels, even when each label occurs twice, is not declared
realizable until all incidence, orientation, crossing, connectedness, and
face-count tests pass.
lem-planar-diagram-code-realizability-an:
## Statement

For a code with a nonempty connected crossing graph, let $C$ be its finite
crossing set, $D$ its darts, $\alpha$ its fixed-point-free edge-pairing
involution, $\sigma$ its clockwise crossing rotation, and
$\phi=\alpha\circ\sigma$ its face permutation. A **spherical realization**
means a polygonal embedding on the oriented sphere whose vertex rotations and
edge pairings are exactly $\sigma$ and $\alpha$; its faces are the cycles of
$\phi$. If every crossing has four darts with the prescribed opposite
over/under pairs, arrows, and sign-consistent cyclic order, then such a
realization exists if and only if $V-E+F=2$, where $V=|C|$, $E=|D|/2$, and
$F$ is the number of cycles of $\phi$. Choosing one face as the outer face
and deleting a point in it gives the corresponding plane realization. The
crossingless one-component code is the single circle and is handled
separately.
alg-planar-code-validation-and-diagram-r:
## Definition

**Input:** A finite tagged Gauss code, signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite code, or
oriented planar-diagram code in the conventions of this page. The crossing
count $c$ is a nonnegative integer. When $c>0$, the code includes the finite
crossing labels, edge-end incidences, strand arrows, over/under data, crossing
signs, and a distinguished outer face. When $c=0$, the only admissible input
for this procedure is the one-component crossingless code specified in the
code definition.

**Output:** Either `Invalid(reason, witness)`, where `reason` is the first
failed check below and `witness` identifies the offending field, label, or
crossing, or `Valid(diagram, components, faces, outerFace)`. Here `diagram` is
a finite gluing record consisting of one crossing disk per vertex, one
rectangular edge band for each pair of darts under $\alpha$, and one cap disk
per cycle of the face permutation. Each band is attached at its recorded dart ports, and each
crossing disk records its clockwise order, strand orientations, over/under
pair, and sign. `components` lists the oriented link cycles, `faces` lists the
face-permutation cycles, and `outerFace` is the selected cycle. The gluing
record represents a polygonal spherical diagram; deleting a point in its
selected face gives the plane model. The procedure tests realizability of
this code only; it does not compare the represented link with another code.

**Instructions:**

1. Read the tag and crossing count. If the tag is unknown or $c$ is not a
   nonnegative integer, return `invalid-header` with that field.

2. If $c=0$, accept only one empty Gauss component word, the empty signed-DT
   code, or the single `Loop[1]` PD record, each with exactly one orientation
   marker, `ccw` or `cw`. Return
   `invalid-crossingless-code` otherwise. For an accepted input return the
   standard circle with the marked orientation, one component, its two sphere
   faces, and the `outside` face selector. Do not run crossing-graph tests.

3. For a Gauss code with $c>0$, reject an empty component word. Check that
   every label lies in $\{1,\ldots,c\}$, occurs exactly twice in total, and
   occurs once with each over/under sign. Check that its separate crossing-sign
   vector has length $c$ and entries in $\{+1,-1\}$. Return
   `invalid-crossing-label` for the first out-of-range label,
   `invalid-crossing-visit-count` with the label and its over/under counts for
   any visit failure, or `invalid-crossing-sign-vector` with the first bad
   position. Turn successive visits on each component word into directed edge
   labels, including each cyclic last-to-first edge, numbering these segments
   in the listed component order and then in traversal order, and form the
   crossing records from the over/under visits and the stored crossing signs.

4. For a signed DT code, check that its pairing list and sign vector each have
   length $c$, each pairing value has absolute value in
   $\{2,4,\ldots,2c\}$, every such absolute value occurs once, and every sign
   is $+1$ or $-1$. Return `invalid-dt-pairing` with the first bad index for a
   pairing failure, or `invalid-crossing-sign-vector` with the first bad
   position for a sign failure. The odd visit $2j-1$ is crossing $j$; if
   $d_j>0$ it is the over-visit and if $d_j<0$ it is the under-visit. At the
   even visit paired with $2j-1$, use crossing label $j$ and the opposite
   over/under sign. Decode visits in order $1,\ldots,2c$ into the corresponding
   signed Gauss word and continue with step 3.

5. For a PD code, check that there are exactly $c$ crossing records and four
   dart occurrences at each record. Return `invalid-crossing-record` with the
   first bad record otherwise. Use the edge labels and arrows in the records
   to form the paired-dart involution, crossing rotations, over/under pairs,
   and crossing signs.

6. In every nonempty encoding, check that each edge label has exactly two
   occurrences, one incoming and one outgoing; each crossing has exactly four
   incident darts; the opposite pairs are exactly one over-strand and one
   under-strand; each strand has one incoming and one outgoing end; and the
   cyclic order matches the stored crossing sign. Return, in that order,
   `invalid-edge-incidence`, `invalid-crossing-valence`,
   `invalid-over-under-pair`, `invalid-strand-orientation`, or
   `invalid-crossing-sign-order`, with the first offending label or crossing.

7. Starting at each as-yet unvisited outgoing dart, cross its edge by $\alpha$
   to the incoming dart at the other endpoint and continue through the
   opposite dart of that same strand. Stop only when the starting outgoing
   dart is reached. If an end is missing, a dart repeats before that return, or
   any dart remains uncovered after all cycles are traced, return
   `invalid-component-closure` with the first such dart. Then test the crossing
   graph for connectedness; if it is disconnected, return
   `disconnected-crossing-graph`.

8. Compute $\phi=\alpha\circ\sigma$ on all darts by finite table lookup and
   list its cycles. Put $V=c$, $E=|D|/2$, and $F=$ the number of cycles. If
   $V-E+F\ne2$, return `non-spherical-face-count` with $(V,E,F)$. If the
   supplied outer-face identifier is not one of these cycles, return
   `invalid-outer-face` with that identifier.

9. For a passing code, choose the lexicographically first spanning tree in the
   finite edge ordering. Root it at the least crossing label and attach its
   tree bands in increasing distance from that root, using the recorded cyclic
   gaps. Then attach the remaining edge bands in increasing edge-label order.
   Use the distinguished face for the plane projection, replace each crossing
   disk by its prescribed transverse crossing, attach one cap disk along each
   face cycle, and lift the over-strand above the under-strand. Return this
   finite gluing record, the directed components, the face cycles, and the
   outer-face identifier.
alg-enumerate-diagrams-up-to-crossing-bo:
## Definition

**Input:** A nonnegative integer crossing bound $N$.

**Output:** A finite ordered list of reconstructed knot-diagram candidates. A
candidate is a `Valid` output of the planar-code validation procedure whose
code is a normalized planar-diagram code with one oriented component and at
most $N$ crossings. Repeated candidates up to crossing relabeling or planar
isotopy are allowed; the list is not a list of knot types.

**Instructions:**

1. If $N$ is not a nonnegative integer, return `invalid-bound`.
2. Initialize the output list empty. Pass the two normalized crossingless
   one-component codes, with `ccw` and `cw` orientation markers in that order,
   through the validator and append both outputs first.
3. For each $c=1,\ldots,N$ in increasing order, use crossing labels
   $\{1,\ldots,c\}$ and the four normalized dart positions at each crossing.
   Enumerate every crossing-sign vector in lexicographic order, with
   $-1<+1$. The sign determines the incoming and outgoing positions at each
   crossing by the normalized-code convention.
4. For each sign vector, enumerate every bijection from the set of its
   $2c$ outgoing darts to its $2c$ incoming darts in lexicographic order.
   Pair each outgoing dart with its image to obtain the edge involution, and
   assign edge labels by the normalized-code rule.
5. Compute the cycles of $\phi=\alpha\circ\sigma$ for each pairing. For each
   cycle, in increasing order of its least dart, select that cycle in turn as
   the outer face and form the corresponding normalized PD code.
6. Pass each code through the planar-code validation procedure. Append its
   reconstructed output if and only if the validator returns `Valid` and the
   directed component tracing has exactly one cycle. Return the list after
   the finite loops end.

This procedure enumerates normalized finite codes and reconstructed diagrams;
it neither identifies equivalent codes nor decides whether two candidates
represent isotopic knots.
thm-planar-code-validation-and-diagram-r:
## Statement

For every finite input in the three code formats, the validation and
reconstruction procedure terminates. It returns an invalid-code reason
exactly when the first failed syntax, incidence, orientation, component,
connectedness, face-count, or outer-face condition in its stated order occurs;
otherwise it returns the crossing-disk/edge-band model of the represented
oriented diagram, its oriented components, its face cycles, and its selected
outer face.
thm-enumerate-diagrams-up-to-crossing-bo:
## Statement

For every nonnegative integer $N$, the bounded enumeration procedure
terminates and returns exactly the reconstructed candidates represented by
normalized connected one-component planar-diagram codes with at most $N$
crossings. Each returned candidate has a valid spherical face structure and a
selected outer face. The procedure does not identify candidates that represent
the same knot type.
thm-valid-code-reconstructs-the-declared:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every valid connected one-component
oriented code with a selected outer face, the reconstruction procedure
produces a regular oriented diagram representing that code. Any two such
diagrams with the same code differ only by crossing and edge relabeling and
are planar isotopic. The normalized planar-diagram code of a diagram with $c$
crossings appears among the candidates enumerated at bound $c$. This statement
concerns diagrams and their finite codes; it does not identify distinct codes
that may represent the same knot type. The finite realization and enumeration
claims are choice-free; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is assumed only for the smooth
ambient-isotopy uniqueness clause.
